Q48755950.summary: In this finely carved ivory panel, three veiled women approach from the lower right, greeted by the angel seated before the tomb, a two-storey building crowned by a domed rotunda, while two guards slump against it. Above, the risen Christ, haloed and holding a scroll, strides up a hill and grasps the hand of God reaching from the clouds, as two disciples below cower or look up in awe. It is one of the oldest known figurative images of the Resurrection and Ascension.
facts: The panel was acquired for the Bavarian National Museum in 1860 from the Bamberg collector Martin von Reider, after whom it is named; it is the oldest work on display in the museum (inv. MA 157).
Drill holes at the four corners suggest it was once set into the cover of a liturgical book.
The tomb building has been discussed as a possible reflection of the shrine over Christ's tomb in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, consecrated in 335.
Q48755950.notes: Date c. 400 and origin Rome or Milan per German Wikipedia and the Commons file description; worklist had '4th century'.

princeton:24185.summary: Framed by spirally fluted columns under a low pediment, a curly-haired young shepherd stands with a sheep slung over his shoulders, smiling slightly as he looks out at the viewer. Two more sheep wait at his feet beside two small trees, and a bird perches in the branches at the left. The slab is a clear, confident example of the Good Shepherd as it was carved on Christian sarcophagi around 300, promising the dead the care of the shepherd who seeks out the lost.
facts: The museum notes the shepherd's practical dress: a belted long-sleeved tunic, laced boots and puttees, wrappings that protected the legs from thorny undergrowth.
The slab was probably cut from the centre of a strigilated sarcophagus, where three relief panels were separated by wavy fluting.
It was bought by Princeton from the dealer Piero Tozzi in Rome in 1952.

walters:71.68.summary: Beneath an arch on slender columns Christ hangs on the cross, his body long and still, his head bowed toward his mother. The Virgin at the left raises her hand in sorrow, and St John at the right lifts his hand toward Christ. Once the centre of a triptych, the plaque now sits in a later fabric-covered mount.
facts: The Walters dates the plaque to the second half of the 10th century and notes that it was originally the centre of a triptych.
Henry Walters bought it in 1925 through the Paris dealer Henri Daguerre.
